# Ledger scale bench

Generated by `scripts/bench-ledger.ts` (`npm run bench:ledger -- --sizes 10000,100000`) against real synthetic
ledgers (`test/gen/synthetic-ledger.ts`), one size at a time, each in its own temp project outside the repo,
deleted after. **Sizes are 10,000 and 100,000 runs only — both real, both measured.** 1,000,000 is never run: the
owner dropped it from the study (fix round 1 of Task 27's report), and separately, Task 27 found that
`generateLedgerRecords`/`toJsonl` hit Node's `buffer.constants.MAX_STRING_LENGTH` (≈512 MiB) somewhere north of
~500,000 records on this build, before a single bench op even runs — so past what's shown below, this doc gives a
*labelled extrapolation* from the 10k→100k slope, never a number claimed as measured (§"1,000,000: extrapolated,
not measured").

Machine for this run: the same shared VM class as Task 27's (24 vCPUs, ~16 GiB RAM, Node v20.19.5 — matching
Task 27's own machine notes closely enough that this looks like the same box), under real load at run time
(`uptime` showed a load average around 4–5, several GiB of swap already in use — other work sharing the
machine) — noted because it directly explains the p95 numbers below, not as an excuse: p50 is the number to
trust here, p95 is discussed with that caveat front and center.

**Bottom line:** the index-backed reuse lookup Task 29 adds turns `lookupAnswers`/`exactReuse` from "crosses 1
full second at 100k" (Task 27's baseline, still-linear) into "tens of milliseconds at p50" — a nearly 15–17×
drop at p50. `checkLedger` (every paid call's ledger gate) and `appendFailedLocked` move off a full log read onto
the same index. One real end-to-end paid `class` call through the fake provider, run for real at each size, comes
in at single-digit-to-low-teens milliseconds — comfortably inside the target. p95 on `lookupAnswers` specifically
is the one number that does *not* cleanly clear the < 100 ms target on this machine, and that section explains
why, with the actual numbers, rather than picking a nicer run.

## Before → after: what Task 29 actually changed, at 100k

Task 27's own bench (same script, same synthetic generator, before this task) is the "before" column; the
`lookupAnswers`/`exactReuse` rows above (after this task's index-backed rewrite) are "after." Both are real,
both are in this repo's history (Task 27's raw numbers are reproduced in full in its own report).

| op | before p50 | before p95 | after p50 | after p95 | p50 speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lookupAnswers | 1183.855 ms | 1453.378 ms | 68.319 ms | 360.843 ms | ≈17.3× |
| exactReuse | 1118.273 ms | 1395.794 ms | 75.119 ms | 89.619 ms | ≈14.9× |
| checkLedger (via `class`, see below) | full `readLedger` every paid call, O(log size) | — | folded into the `class` row below | — | — |
| append | 239.226 ms | 239.226 ms | 290.855 ms | 290.855 ms | — |
| nextRunNumber / findRun | 50.136 / 47.409 ms | 62.800 / 59.633 ms | 83.169 / 81.657 ms | 124.200 / 110.110 ms | unchanged code |

`nextRunNumber`/`findRun` didn't change in this task — Task 27 already put them on the index — and their "after"
numbers land noticeably *higher* than Task 27's own baseline for the exact same code path. That's the loaded
machine, not a regression: see the p95 section below for the fuller argument, and note the same signature
(everything roughly 1.5–2× Task 27's own numbers for unchanged ops) shows up in `append` too, which also didn't
change. Read `lookupAnswers`/`exactReuse`'s 14–17× *p50* improvement as the real signal — it survives the noise
because "linear scan of 100k lines" vs "index lookup" isn't a close call at any load level.

`checkLedger` and `appendFailedLocked` (log.ts) moved off `readLedger` (a full read-and-validate of the whole
log, every single paid call) onto `loadIndex` (validate only the bytes after the index's `upto` — typically zero,
once the index is warm) plus a small targeted `checkTail` check for a truly in-progress append (see "What earned
its place," below, for why that second piece exists). There's no isolated "before" number for `checkLedger` alone
in Task 27's bench (it didn't touch the index then), so its improvement is captured indirectly, in the `class`
row: a full paid call — `checkLedger` + `lookupAnswers` + the actual append, run for real, through the fake
provider — comes in at 8.6 ms (10k) and 2.4 ms (100k), comfortably inside the < 100 ms target, at *both* sizes.
(The 100k number being smaller than the 10k one is not a mistake: this specific measurement's `who` is the fake
provider, which has zero prior history in the synthetic ledger at any size, so `lookupAnswers`/`exactReuse` both
return instantly regardless of ledger size — see "What earned its place" for what this does and doesn't prove.)

## The p95 number that doesn't clearly clear target, and why

`lookupAnswers`'s p95 at 100k is 360.843 ms in the run above — over the < 100 ms target — while its own p50 (68.3
ms) and `exactReuse`'s p95 (89.6 ms, right at target) are fine. A second full run, minutes later on the same
loaded machine, gave `lookupAnswers` p95 = 303.512 ms and `exactReuse` p95 = 101.204 ms — both runs miss or
graze the target on p95, neither cleanly clears it, and **`findRun`'s p95 also moved from Task 27's 59.6 ms
baseline to 110–197 ms across these two runs, on code this task never touched.** That's the tell: with only 20
samples per O(n) op (`O_N_SAMPLE_CAP`, inherited from Task 27), p95 is effectively "the single worst of 20
trials" — on a machine with a load average of 4–5 and multiple GiB of swap in active use, one GC pause or
scheduler preemption during that worst trial is enough to blow the number, and it happens to unrelated,
unchanged operations too. p50 (68–91 ms across the two runs, comfortably under target both times) is the number
this doc trusts for "did the change work"; p95 on this specific machine, at this sample count, is reported
honestly rather than smoothed over, and the owner's escalation path (a sorted fixed-width fallback file) was not
reached for because the *algorithm* isn't the bottleneck here — a quieter machine or a larger sample count would
very likely clear it too, and neither of those is a Task 29 code change.

## 1,000,000: extrapolated, not measured

Not run, by owner decision (Task 27's fix round 1) and, independently, because it doesn't fit through the current
`toJsonl` interface on this Node build (Task 27's finding: `MAX_STRING_LENGTH` ≈512 MiB, crossed somewhere north
of ~500k records). Extrapolating linearly from the two real points above (`rebuild`, the one operation that's
still a genuine full scan by design, scales with total log size): log bytes grow ~10× from 10k→100k
(10,256,591 → 102,639,749), so a 1,000,000-run ledger would be on the order of **~1 GB of log** and, at the
measured `indexBytes/logBytes` ratio (~3%, see below), **~30 MB of index.json** — both estimates, not
measurements. `rebuild`'s own p50 grew from 139.8 ms to 3,211.9 ms across the same 10× step (a ~23× increase,
noisier than a clean 10× given the machine load discussed above), so a 1M rebuild would land somewhere in the
tens of seconds. None of this is a claim this doc stands behind as measured; it's the shape a reader would expect
before ever running it.

## Compaction cadence: `REBUILD_SIZE_RATIO`

`loadIndex` (`src/ledger/index.ts`) rebuilds from scratch instead of patching once `index.json` exceeds
`REBUILD_SIZE_RATIO` of `log.jsonl`'s size — two `statSync` calls, checked right where `loadIndex` already
decides stale-vs-catch-up. The real run above gives the actual ratio at both measured sizes:

| n | index bytes | log bytes | indexBytes / logBytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10,000 | 299,054 | 10,256,591 | 0.0292 |
| 100,000 | 3,136,052 | 102,639,749 | **0.0306** |

**`REBUILD_SIZE_RATIO = 0.05`** — the smallest round number (multiples of 0.05) at or above 0.0306, the ratio at
the largest size actually measured (the 100,000-run row above). This gives roughly 1.6× headroom over what was
observed, without being so loose that a genuinely bloated index (many more distinct providers or a much larger
distinct-key pool than this bench's ~168-key synthetic mix) goes unnoticed. Task 27's baseline ratio (before this
task's `reuseKey`/`runIdsNewestFirst` fields) was ~1.9–2.1%; this task's added fields pushed it to ~2.9–3.1% —
still small, still cheap to throw away and rebuild, which is the property that matters: a full rebuild is one
linear pass and a few lines of code, and incrementally garbage-collecting a map that only ever grows (`runOffset`,
`blocked`, `runIdsNewestFirst` — all keyed by run id, so none of them can shrink without breaking a lookup for
some still-valid historical id) isn't worth building for a file that's disposable by design.

## What earned its place, and what didn't

**Earned it:** `LedgerIndex.runIdsNewestFirst` (`"<adapter>|<model>" -> run ids, newest first`) is what actually
backs `lookupAnswers`/`exactReuse` now — a newest-to-oldest walk scoped to the matching provider, using
`readRecordAt` against offsets already in memory (never re-loading the index per candidate, which was a real bug
caught during development: an earlier draft called `findRun` per candidate, which calls `loadIndex` internally,
turning a scan of a few hundred candidates into a few hundred re-reads and re-parses of `index.json` — minutes,
not milliseconds, for the correctness test below at just 6,000 runs). This is the piece that produces the
14–17× p50 improvement above. `LedgerIndex.reuseKey` (`"<adapter>|<model>" -> answerKey -> newest holder`) is
populated exactly as specified — self-compacting, one entry per distinct key ever asked, not per run — and backs
an O(1) fast path inside `lookupAnswers` for the common case (a key whose current holder isn't blocked), which is
most of why `lookupAnswers`'s p50 (68–91 ms) sits close to `nextRunNumber`/`findRun`'s (83–84 ms) rather than
meaningfully above it, despite doing strictly more work per call. `checkTail` (log.ts) is a small, deliberately
narrow piece: the id index tolerates a trailing incomplete line as "might still be writing" (right for readers
like `view`/`findRun`), but a writer's `checkLedger`/`appendFailedLocked` needs the stricter behavior
`readLedger` always had — an in-progress append from another process must make a new write refuse, not proceed.
Skipping this was caught by an existing e2e test (`dependencies.test.ts`'s truncated-tail case), not by
inspection — worth naming, since it's exactly the kind of gap a bench number never shows.

**Didn't earn a use, but stayed:** `reuseKey` is *not* the read path for `exactReuse` — it can't be, safely.
`reuseKey` stores a key's *origin* (resolved through `reusedFrom`), but `exactReuse` must return the id of the
matching run *itself* (Task 11's own contract: `return r.id`, not its reuse origin). Once a run reuses a key
rather than asking it fresh, its own id is discarded the moment `reuseKey` is overwritten by whoever touches that
key next — there is nowhere left to recover it from. A shortcut here would return the wrong run precisely when a
real reuse chain exists, and — worse — would look correct against this task's own scale test, since the
synthetic generator (`test/gen/synthetic-ledger.ts`) never populates `reusedFrom` at all, so every generated run
is trivially its own origin. `exactReuse` stays the full newest-first scan; `reuseKey` stays populated (it
satisfies the documented `LedgerIndex` shape, and a future caller that reads a candidate's own record rather than
trusting a stored qid could still use it as a starting point) but unread by `exactReuse`. Full reasoning and the
qid-mismatch case that ruled out the more obvious shortcut is in `src/ledger/reuse.ts`'s file header.

**Noted, not fixed:** `nextRunNumber`/`findRun` (log.ts, unchanged since Task 27) each call `loadIndex`
independently — every paid call now makes three separate `loadIndex` calls in sequence (`checkLedger`,
`lookupAnswers`, `nextRunNumber`), each re-reading and `JSON.parse`-ing the whole (warm, unchanged) `index.json`
from scratch rather than sharing one already-loaded copy across the request. At 100k that file is ~3 MB; OS page
cache keeps the repeated reads cheap enough that the `class` row above still lands well under target, but it's
real, measurable redundant work. Threading a single loaded `LedgerIndex` through `checkLedger` → `lookupAnswers`
→ `nextRunNumber` within one request would remove it, but that means changing the call signatures of
functions used across every verb (`pay.ts`, `class.ts`, `sweep.ts`, `drill.ts`, `change.ts`) — not a cheap,
scannable-diff change, so per the brief's own instruction ("fix only if cheap") it's documented here instead of
attempted. `rebuild`'s cost (a genuine full linear scan, only paid on a missing/corrupt/stale index) is the other
number worth keeping an eye on at real project scale — see the 1M extrapolation above.
